seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: I hope Mrs Pound is better by now. The ice saints came too soon this year – a rare case of punctuality in these parts. Many thanks for your kind invitation and proposal to meet Mr Eliot. As it seems you will not pass this way I shall do my best to get over to you for a few days. The Oxen of the Sun episode is finished but the typing is still a job. As soon as it is ready will post it you express to be sent on to New York and to Miss Weaver as it is overdue. Mr Watson wrote me a month ago about the Dial
and I sent him some verses. Ulysses leaves me no time for sleep much less for other work so that for the moment it is very doubtful if I can send more but I shall try. However, unless the Little Review decides to suspend publication of Ulysses I think it ought to go there as usual. Have you seen
Convegno and Poesia
with some verses of yours? Did you receive Mr Benco’s article on Tarr which I sent you to Venice? It is like hide and seek. On Tuesday I sent you a review to London and on Wednesday I receive your card from Venice. On Sunday I write you to Venice (a city which I have never seen, by the way, though I have lived opposite it for 15 years) and on Monday you write me en route for Sirmione! I shall be glad of a rest of a day or two. This episode has cost me about a thousand hours of work. Thank the Lord it is finished. Apart from this I think it would be too bad if you came so far and went away without our meeting. I hope the lake air agrees with you. If you had come you could have had sea fish – perhaps the only thing left that is still good. Send me a view of the place, please. I saw it several times from the train, I suppose. Travelling is very unpleasant at present, is it not?
I shall get on with the typing as quickly as possible and send off the script. E allora, porca miseria, che dio mandi un accidente a Ulisse, su’ moglie e quelle maledettissime bestiacce del sole .

seg.foreign: Arrivederci – o piuttosto a vederci presto

div.note: In the margin of the first of the two pages of this letter, there are arithmetic calculations in what appears to be Pound’s hand. These may relate to his offer to help JJ with any “fiscal uncertainty” that might prevent him from visiting Sirmione. He wrote JJ on 19 May 1920: “cd. probably reimburse you with some form of sec ou liquide negotiable in Trieste” (Pound/Joyce 166).

Dorothy Shakespear (1886-1973) was an English artist who married Pound in 1914. The Pounds had arrived in Venice in late April 1920 at the start of a planned spring vacation in Italy. On 8 May, Pound reported to JJ that the “Venetian air” had made Dorothy ill and so they were “ignominiously retreating to Lago di Garda at earliest possible date” (Pound/Joyce 164). By 13 May, Pound was writing JJ from Sirmione at Lake Garda and urging him to join them for a week “‘on me,’ as my guest, or whatever the phrase is” (Pound/Joyce 165). On 19 May – in what is certainly a reply to the present letter by JJ, despite the closeness of dates – Pound reported that Dorothy had “considerably recovered” (Pound/Joyce 167).
The “ice saints” is a name given in parts of Europe to Saints Mamertus, Pancras, and Servatius whose feast days fall in May during a period associated with late frosts and cold weather.

On 13 May 1920, Pound invited JJ to join him and Dorothy in Sirmione for a week, “as my guest.” He also hoped that T.S. Eliot (1888-1965) might be persuaded to “take his holiday here,” though he thought it an “extremely doubtful conjunction” (Pound/Joyce 165). Pound had first stayed at Sirmione on Lago di Garda in northern Italy in 1910, almost precisely ten years earlier and in the same accommodations – the Hotel Eden – where he and Dorothy were now installed. With its literary associations going back to Catullus, the lake had become for Pound a mystical, paradisal spot and is a recurrent setting in his Cantos and other poems. In his early poem “The Flame,” Pound wrote of Lake Garda: “Who can look on that blue and not believe?” (Personae: The Shorter Poems, ed. Lea Baechler and A. Walton Litz [New York: New Directions, 1990], 49).

After railway strikes and other delays, JJ and his son Giorgio arrived at Desenzano, a railway stop near Sirmione, on the evening of 8 June 1920, where Pound met them and took them to Sirmione where he and Dorothy were staying at the Hotel Eden.

After the first portion of “Oxen of the Sun,” the fourteenth episode of Ulysses, had appeared in The Little Review, vol. 7, no. 3 (September-December 1920): 81-92, the magazine’s editors were convicted of publishing obscenity (the portion of the “Nausicaa” episode in the July-August 1920 number), and the serialization of Ulysses ended.

As JJ completed episodes of Ulysses, he had copies typed and sent to Pound, who reviewed and transmitted them to New York for serial publication in The Little Review, and to Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961), editor of The Egoist in London. Because of English printers’ fears, The Egoist never consistently serialized Ulysses, and published only a few episodes: “Nestor,” “Proteus,” “Hades,” and part of “Wandering Rocks.” On 19 May 1920, Pound wrote JJ, in expectation of his imminent visit: “Better bring your ‘Oxen’ with you by hand, unless they are already typed” (Pound/Joyce 166). Pound sent one typed copy of “Oxen” to The Little Review from Sirmione on 9 June, and kept the other to take with him to Paris, “as The Egoist isn’t printing it” (Pound/Joyce 173; LIII 28).

The New York magazine The Dial, vol. 69, no. 1 (July 1920): 26, published JJ’s poem, “A Memory of the Players in a Mirror at Midnight,” later included in his volume, Pomes Penyeach (1927). At this time, Pound was becoming a paid European agent and correspondent of The Dial, which had been purchased by two wealthy Harvard alumni, Scofield Thayer (1889-1982) and his friend, James Sibley Watson, Jr. (1894-1982). It may have been Thayer, not Watson, who wrote to Joyce inviting him to contribute. They hoped to make it “a cosmopolitan monthly magazine of literature and the arts,” but they cautioned Pound that they would retain editorial control and would avoid any “honourable martyrization” for publishing offensive matter (A. David Moody, Ezra Pound: Poet, A Portrait of the Man and his Work, vol. 1 [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007], 390-91). In the years that followed, The Dial published important avant-garde work, including poems by W.B. Yeats, D.H. Lawrence, Amy Lowell, William Carlos Williams, Wallace Stevens, and Marianne Moore, as well as T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land and several of Pound’s cantos.

Pound urged JJ to send to The Dial “anything save ‘Ulysses’” on which he might be working, adding that he was hoping to make the magazine “a new Cititatem Dei [sic; City of God]” but cautioning that “they can’t on any account risk suppression by p.o. [post office] authorities” (Pound/Joyce 164).

JJ’s worry that The Little Review might suspend the serialization of Ulysses arose from the fact that the U.S. postal authorities in New York had already suppressed three numbers containing portions of the work: January 1919 (the first part of the “Lestrygonians” episode), May 1919 (the second half of “Scylla and Charybdis”), and January 1920 (the third installment of “Cyclops”). The Post Office effected these suppressions by revoking the offending issues’ second-class postage privileges and declaring the issues “non-mailable” under section 211 of the U.S. penal laws (Paul Vanderham, James Joyce and Censorship: The Trials of Ulysses [London: Macmillan, 1998], 1-2). Pound repeatedly decried this criminal provision as “the amazing, grotesque, and unthinkable, ambiguous law of our country” (“The Classics ‘Escape,’” The Little Review, vol. 4, no. 11 [March 1918]: 33).

note.p: The Milan review Poesia, vol. 1, no. 1 (15 April 1920): 22, reprinted Pound’s poem, “The Study in Aesthetics,” originally published in Poetry magazine for August 1914. The combined number 5-6 of Poesia (August-September 1920) contained an essay, “Ezra Pound,” by the Italian writer and translator, Carlo Linati (1878–1949), along with a bibliography and several of Pound’s poems (11-17). Poesia, vol. 1, nos. 7-9 (October-December 1920): 38, reprinted three poems by Pound, “Difference of opinion with Ligdamus [sic],” “The return,” and “New York.” Issues of the Milan review Il Convegno from this period do not appear to contain any of Pound’s writings, though Linati’s introduction to his translation of JJ’s Exiles (see below) briefly mentions Pound’s critical writing on JJ.

Poesia, vol. 1, no. 1 (15 April 1920): 27, also published JJ’s poem, “A Memory of the Players in a Mirror at Midnight,” later included in his volume, Pomes Penyeach (1927). JJ had sent the verses to Linati circa 9 March 1920 (LI 138). Linati also translated Exiles into Italian as Esuli and published it in Il Convegno, vol. 1, nos. 3-5 (April, May, June 1920): 27-52, 27-46, 22–37. In addition, he published a translation of JJ’s short story “Araby” in Il Convegno, vol. 5, no. 5 (May 1924): 301-08, and excerpts from Ulysses (selected by Pound) in the same journal, vol. 7, nos. 11-12 (November-December 1926): 813-28. (In May 1920, Pound was hoping that Linati might come from Milan and join him and JJ at Sirmione [Pound/Joyce 166]. This did not materialize, and Pound and JJ wrote him a joint letter from Sirmione on 9 June 1920 [LII 469-71].)

Il Convegno: Rivista di letteratura e di arte was founded in Milan in 1920 by theater director and critic, Enzo Ferrieri (1890-1969), and ran until 1940. Ferrieri also established Circolo del Convegno, a club for literary and cultural debate which hosted two lectures on JJ during the 1920s. Poesia (1905-1909), founded in Milan by F.T. Marinetti (1876-1944) to promote modern poetry from many countries, became an important vehicle for Futurism. The review was revived in April 1920 under the editorship of Mario Dessy (1902-1979) to continue the message of Futurism and to engage with other avant-garde movements, but the resuscitated review lasted only a few issues. For a discussion of Il Convegno and Poesia in the context of modern poetry, little magazines, and internationalism, see Eric Bulson, Little Magazine, World Form (New York, NY: Columbia University Press, 2017), 126-39.

div.note: Silvio Benco (1874-1949), Italian writer, journalist, and critic, came to know JJ in Trieste and assisted with three articles that JJ wrote in Italian for the Trieste newspaper Il Piccolo della Sera in 1907: “Il Fenianismo, L’Ultimo Feniano” [“Fenianism: The Last Fenian”], “Home Rule Maggiorenne” [“Home Rule Comes of Age”], and “L’Irlanda alla Sbarra” [“Ireland at the Bar”] (CW 187-200). Benco reviewed the Vorticist novel Tarr, by the English writer and painter Wyndham Lewis (1882-1957), in the Trieste journal La Nazione della Domenica (25 April 1920): 2. Pound greatly admired Tarr, which was initially serialized in the London magazine The Egoist (1916-1917) and later published as a book (1918). He wrote JJ on 19 May 1920 that he had received Benco’s review of Tarr from JJ and was forwarding it to Lewis (Pound/Joyce 166).
Possibly Pound’s postcard to JJ dated 3 May 1920 from Albergo Pilsen-Manin, Venice (Pound/Joyce 164).

Pound replied by urging JJ to “stop a night in Venice on your way back to Trieste …. S. Marco is worth looking at” (Pound/Joyce 167). In early July 1920, JJ visited Venice for two days on his way to Paris (Ellmann, JJ 482).

Possibly Pound’s letter to JJ of 8 May 1920 in which he noted that he and his wife Dorothy were leaving Venice for Lake Garda on Sirmione (Pound/Joyce 164-65). However, 8 May 1920 was a Saturday, not a Monday.

Pound replied, “There ain’t no real views [of Sirmione on Lake Garda],” but then proceeded to enclose some images along with attempts by his wife Dorothy, a painter, to sketch “the colour scheme from the end of the peninsula … all I can say is that the water is quite as blue at times as the bluest part of the paint” (Pound/Joyce 167). Although this letter is dated 19 May 1920, it plainly replies to JJ’s letter of 18 May.
“And then, bloody hell, may god send a curse on Ulysses, his wife and those blasted bleeding beasts of the sun.”
“See you later – or rather see you soon.”
